'''''Phaseolus acutifolius''''', also known as the '''tepary bean''', is a [[legume]] native to the [[southwestern United States]] and [[Mexico]] that has been grown there by the native peoples since [[Pre-Columbian era|pre-Columbian times]]. It is more [[drought-resistant]] than the [[common bean]] (''Phaseolus vulgaris'') and is grown in desert and semi-desert conditions from [[Arizona]] through Mexico to [[Costa Rica]]. The water requirements are low. The crop will grow in areas where annual rainfall is less than {{convert|400|mm|in|abbr=on}}.

== Description ==
The tepary bean is an annual and can be climbing, trailing, or erect, with stems up to {{convert|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} long. The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]], {{lang|la|acutifolius}}, is derived from [[Latin]] {{lang|la|acutus}} {{gloss|pointed, acute}}, and {{lang|la|-folius}} {{gloss|-leaved}}.<ref name="Eggli Newton 200422">{{cite encyclopedia |year=2004|title=acutifolius|encyclopedia=Etymological Dictionary of Succulent Plant Names|publisher=Springer|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u2n5vusQ1DEC&pg=PA2|access-date=19 November 2018|page=2|isbn=978-3-540-00489-9|last2=Newton|first2=Leonard E.|last1=Eggli|first1=Urs}}</ref> A narrow leafed, variety ''tenuifolius'', and a broader leafed, variety ''latifolius'', are known. Domestic varieties are derived from ''latifolius''. Observation of "a limited number" of wild specimens suggested that "the flowers concur with the summer rains, first appearing in late August, with the pods ripening early in the fall dry season, most of them in October".<ref name="NaFe197822">{{cite journal |author-link=Gary Paul Nabhan|date=Jan–Mar 1978|title=Teparies in Southwestern North America: A Biogeographical and Ethnohistorical Study of Phaseolus acutifolius|journal=[[Economic Botany]]|volume=32|issue=1|pages=2–19|jstor=4253886|author1-surname=Nabhan|author1-given=Gary P.|author2-surname=Felger|author2-given=Richard S.}}</ref>{{rp|6}} The beans can be of nearly any color. There are many local [[Landrace|landraces]]. Beans vary in size but tend to be small. They mature 60 to 120 days after planting.<ref>{{cite web |title=Phaseolus acutifolius A. Gray|url=http://www.prota4u.org/protav8.asp?h=M4&t=Phaseolus,acutifolius&p=Phaseolus+acutifolius|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220034242/http://www.prota4u.org/protav8.asp?h=M4&t=Phaseolus,acutifolius&p=Phaseolus+acutifolius|archive-date=2016-12-20|access-date=2012-07-09|work=PROTA4U.org}}</ref>

Other names for this native bean include '''Pawi''', '''Pavi''', '''Tepari''', '''Escomite''', '''Yori mui''', '''Yorimuni''' and '''Yori muni'''. The name ''tepary'' may derive from the [[Tohono O'odham]] phrase {{lang|ood|tʼpawi}} or "It's a bean".<ref name="AgIndia22">{{cite web |title=Tepary Bean|url=http://www.agriculturalproductsindia.com/cereals-pulses/cereals-tepary-bean.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120706102537/http://www.agriculturalproductsindia.com/cereals-pulses/cereals-tepary-bean.html|archive-date=2012-07-06|access-date=2012-07-08|website=agriculturalproductsindia.com|publisher=Agro Products}}</ref> The name for a small bean was recorded in the 17th century, in the now extinct [[Eudeve language]] of northern Mexico, as ''{{lang|opt|tépar}}'' ([[accusative case]], ''{{lang|opt|tépari}}'').<ref>{{cite book |last=Pennington|first=Campbell W.|title=Arte y vocabulario de la lengua dohema, heve o eudeva|publisher=UNAM|year=1981|place=Mexico City|page=230|language=es}}</ref> Names that contain {{lang|opt|yori}} in them typically refer to non-native species of beans, since those names mean "non-Indian person's bean".<ref>{{cite book |last1=Felger|first1=Richard Stephen|title=People of the Desert and Sea: Ethnobotany of the Seri Indians|last2=Beck Moser|first2=Mary|publisher=University of Arizona Press|year=1985|isbn=|place=Tucson|page=342}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==

=== History ===
Tepary beans have been grown by [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]] for thousands of years; cultivated beans have been found dating to 500 BCE in the [[Tehuacán]] Valley in Mexico. Tepary beans appear to have been domesticated in a single event in northern Mexico, based on genetic evidence.<ref name=":022">{{Cite web |last=Gray|first=A.|date=September 2018|title=Plant Guide for Tepary Bean, Phaseolu acutifolius|url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/cs-pg_phac.pdf|website=plants.[[USDA]].gov|publisher=[[Natural Resources Conservation Service]]}}</ref>

The Sand Papago ([[Hia C-eḍ O'odham]]) were mainly hunter-gatherers but cultivated tepary beans and other crops when moisture made it possible for them to do so. In 1912, ethnographer [[Carl Lumholtz]] found small cultivated fields primarily of tepary beans in the [[Pinacate Peaks]] area of Sonora. In the Pinacate, with an average annual precipitation of {{convert|75|mm|in|abbr=on}} and temperatures up to {{convert|48|°C|°F|abbr=on}}, Tohono O'Odham and Mexican farmers utilized runoff from sparse rains to grow crops. In the 1980s, author [[Gary Paul Nabhan]] visited this area, and found one farm family taking advantage of the first large rain in six years, planting seeds in the wet ground and harvesting a crop two months later. The most successful crops were tepary beans and a drought-adapted squash. Nabhan calculated that the cultivation in the Pinacate was the most arid area in the world where rain-fed agriculture is practiced.<ref>{{cite book |last=Nabhan|first=Gary Paul|title=Gathering the Desert|publisher=University of Arizona Press|year=1990|isbn=|place=Tucson|pages=107–116}}</ref>

The tepary bean was a major food staple of natives in the Southwestern United States and northern Mexico. In addition to being grown in floodplains, it was often grown alongside squash and corn. Growing these plants together, known as [[Three Sisters (agriculture)|Three Sisters agriculture]], enhances their growth and provides more balanced nutrition.

In the United States, the tepary bean was introduced to Anglo farmers in the 19th century by [[Tohono O'Odham]] (Papago) farmers.{{r|NaFe197822|p=8–15}} The Native American method of planting in the American Southwest was to plant three to five seeds in hills {{convert|6 to 8|feet}} apart. Beans were planted in [[Arroyo (watercourse)|arroyos]] that had been recently flooded by summer rain.<ref>{{cite journal |date=July–August 1983|title=Tepary: the Bean that Laughs at Drought|url=http://www.motherearthnews.com/Organic-Gardening/1983-07-01/Teparty-The-Bean-that-Laughs-at-Drought.aspx|journal=Mother Earth News|access-date=2012-07-08}}</ref>

=== Cropping systems ===
The tepary bean is traditionally sown at the start of the [[monsoon]] season, typically from mid-June to mid-July. With access to [[irrigation]], earlier seeding dates are possible. [[Seed|Seeds]] are generally planted 2.5–4 cm deep. Row spacing ranges from 30–40 cm in small-scale plantings and 70―80 cm in larger operations. Seeding rates typically vary between  25 and 35 kg per hectare, with approximately 9000 seeds per kilogramm.

Tepary beans are very drought-tolerant. Nevertheless [[Germination]] requires wet soil. Once established, the plants will flourish in dry conditions.<ref name=":022" /> Excessive water will impair crop development and may lead to increased vegetative growth at the expense of seed [[Crop yield|yield]]. Thus irrigation after germination is commonly limitied to situations, where plants show significant [[Moisture stress|water stress]]. The Tepary bean has a positive impact on [[soil fertility]], as it is forming [[symbiosis]] with nitrogen-fixing bacteria ([[Rhizobia]]), like other legumes. The Rhizobia fix [[nitrogen]] gas (N<sub>2</sub>) from the atmosphere, turning it into a plant-available form. This property of adding nitrogen to the soil makes legumes attractive for low-input systems. <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nong|first1=Refilwe A.|last2=Gerrano|first2=Abe S.|last3=Gwata|first3=Eastonce T.|title=Impact of soil moisture stress on growth and physiological traits of tepary bean genotypes|journal=Journal of Underutilised Crops Research|date=4 April 2025|volume=4|issue=1|pages=10|doi=10.4102/jucr.v4i1.26|url=https://doi.org/10.4102/jucr.v4i1.26|access-date=9 November 2025|language=en|issn=2958-0994|doi-access=free}}</ref> Plant residues after harvest can contain up to 150kg nitrogen per hectar. <ref>{{Cite web|title=10/ Düngung im Gemüsebau / GRUD 2017|url=https://www.agrarforschungschweiz.ch/2017/06/10-duengung-im-gemuesebau-grud-2017/|website=Agrarforschung Schweiz|date=2017-06-01|access-date=2025-11-27|language=de-DE|first=Simone|last=Zaugg}}</ref>

[[Fertilizer|Fertilization]] and [[pest control]] are similar to those for the common bean. [[Agroscope]], the Swiss center for agricultural research, indicates fertilization of no nitrogen, 8.7kg [[Phosphorus|phoshorus]] and 58.1kg [[potassium]] per hectar for the common bean. <ref>{{Cite web|title=10/ Düngung im Gemüsebau / GRUD 2017|url=https://www.agrarforschungschweiz.ch/2017/06/10-duengung-im-gemuesebau-grud-2017/|website=Agrarforschung Schweiz|date=2017-06-01|access-date=2025-11-27|language=de-DE|first=Simone|last=Zaugg}}</ref> Diseases in most beans include Anthracnose, Blights and rots, as well as Rust.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Genetic Resources, Chromosome Engineering, and Crop Improvement: Grain Legumes, Volume I|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rzL-i0fVMuoC&dq=phaseolus+vulgaris+diseases&pg=PA11|publisher=CRC Press|date=2005-03-16|isbn=978-0-203-48928-4|language=en|first1=Ram J.|last1=Singh|first2=Prem P.|last2=Jauhar}}</ref>

Beans can be harvested after 60 to 120 days, depending on environmental conditions. Harvest can be done via cutting, windrowing and then combining. Yields generally range from 400–800 kg/ha in drylands and 900–1700 kg/ha in systems with irrigation (adjusted to the needs of the tepary bean). Reports on historical tepary bean yields in the United States vary widely. In [[Aridity|arid regions]], yields recorded between 1910 and 1975 ranged from under 200 kg/ha to just over 2,000 kg/ha, depending on irrigation availability. In contrast yields may surpass 4,630 kg/ha in regions with less extreme climate conditions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Nabhan|first1=Gary P.|last2=Felger|first2=Richard S.|year=1978|title=Teparies in Southwestern North America|journal=Economic Botany|volume=32|issue=1|pages=3–19|doi=10.1007/bf02906725}}</ref>

=== Relevance ===
Northwestern Mexico is the primary area of production for tepary beans. The tepary is also cultivated in many countries in Africa, Australia, and Asia. In India, tepary beans are an ingredient in the snacks "[[bhujia]]" and Punjabi Tadka by [[Haldiram's]].<ref name="AgIndia2">{{cite web |title=Tepary Bean|url=http://www.agriculturalproductsindia.com/cereals-pulses/cereals-tepary-bean.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120706102537/http://www.agriculturalproductsindia.com/cereals-pulses/cereals-tepary-bean.html|archive-date=2012-07-06|access-date=2012-07-08|website=agriculturalproductsindia.com|publisher=Agro Products}}</ref>

{{As of|2015}}, the [[International Center for Tropical Agriculture]] in [[Colombia]] is testing [[Crossbreed|crossbreeds]] of the tepary bean and [[common bean]], in order to impart the tepary's drought and heat resistance. The latter could be especially helpful given [[Global warming|climate change]]'s effects on agriculture.<ref>{{cite news |last=Charles|first=Dan|date=25 March 2015|title=Meet The Cool Beans Designed To Beat Climate Change|url=https://www.npr.org/blogs/thesalt/2015/03/25/395096885/meet-the-cool-beans-designed-to-beat-climate-change|access-date=25 March 2015|website=[[NPR]].org}}</ref>

=== Heat stress resistance ===
''P. acutifolius'' is a sister species of ''P. vulgaris''; genomic studies estimate that it diverged from ''P. vulgaris'' around ~2.1 Mya. As part of this divergence, the species duplicated genes that supported resistance to abiotic stress in arid zones: binding genes coding for chitin-binding proteins, kinase activity, cell wall macromolecule catabolic/metabolic processes and amino sugar metabolism (Example: [[Glucosamine]]). The tepary bean uses these amino sugars as a protection mechanism against heat stress, preventing proteins within the body of the plant from starting a denaturation process.<ref name=":122">{{Cite journal |last1=Moghaddam|first1=Samira Mafi|last2=Oladzad|first2=Atena|last3=Koh|first3=Chushin|last4=Ramsay|first4=Larissa|last5=Hart|first5=John P.|last6=Mamidi|first6=Sujan|last7=Hoopes|first7=Genevieve|last8=Sreedasyam|first8=Avinash|last9=Wiersma|first9=Andrew|last10=Zhao|first10=Dongyan|last11=Grimwood|first11=Jane|display-authors=3|date=2021-05-11|title=The tepary bean genome provides insight into evolution and domestication under heat stress|journal=Nature Communications|language=en|volume=12|issue=1|page=2638|bibcode=2021NatCo..12.2638M|doi=10.1038/s41467-021-22858-x|issn=2041-1723|pmc=8113540|pmid=33976152|s2cid=234472801}}</ref>

A study, published in 2021, showed that when the tepary bean plant is exposed to high temperatures there is a negative regulation of the genes involved in cell division ([http://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0048523 GO:0048523]; [http://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0045786 GO:0045786]) and a positive regulation of those involved in arrest ([http://amigo.geneontology.org/amigo/term/GO:0051726 GO: 0007050]). This suggests that above 37°C cells that are in the cell division cycle is arrested in the G1-S phase; it seems that this is done by the cell in order to avoid the development of organism and thus conserve energy. [[Trehalose]] synthesis genes were also found to be overexpressed; trehalose is a sugar that in high concentrations is capable of protecting cell membranes and proteins from the denaturation process. A [[synteny]] analysis revealed that there is an intrachromosomal rearrangement on chromosomes 2 and 9; this could be a factor in the difficulties in developing fertile hybrids.<ref name=":122" />

Not only are tepary beans more resistant to heat and drought stress than [[common beans]] (''Phaseolus vulgaris''), they are also reported to tolerate mild subzero temperatures better under field conditions. The survival rate of tepary beans seven days after mild frost events has been found to be significantly higher than that of [[common beans]]. <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Souter|first1=J. R.|last2=Gurusamy|first2=V.|last3=Porch|first3=T. G.|last4=Bett|first4=K. E.|year=2017|title=Successful introgression of abiotic stress tolerance from wild tepary bean to common bean|journal=Crop Science|volume=57|issue=3|pages=1160–1171|doi=10.2135/cropsci2016.10.0851|doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Nutritional aspects ==
The nutritional characteristics of the tepary bean are generally similar to those of the [[common bean]] (''Phaseolus vulgaris''). Like other [[legumes]], tepary beans are rich in [[protein]].<ref name="Thorn1983">{{cite journal |last1=Thorn|first1=K. A.|last2=Tinsley|first2=A. M.|last3=Weber|first3=C. W.|last4=Berry|first4=J. W.|year=1983|title=Antinutritional Factors in Legumes of the Sonoran Desert|journal=Ecology of Food and Nutrition|volume=13|issue=4 |pages=251–256|doi=10.1080/03670244.1983.9990757 |bibcode=1983EcoFN..13..251T |hdl=10150/557677|hdl-access=free}}</ref> They contain 15–32% protein, 0.9–1.7% fat, and 65.3–69.1% carbohydrate.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Osman|first=MA|year=2002|title=Thermal inactivation of tepary bean (Phaseolus acutifolius), soybean and lima bean protease inhibitors: Effect of acidic and basic pH|journal=Food Chemistry|volume=78|issue=4|pages=419–423|doi=10.1016/S0308-8146(02)00144-9|bibcode=2002FoodC..78..419O |url=https://doi.org/10.1016/S0308-8146(02)00144-9|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Total dietary fiber content ranges from 18–21%, of which 0.5–1% are considered soluble fiber and 17–20% insoluble fiber.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sathe|first=SK|year=1994|title=Purification and biochemical characterization of tepary bean (Phaseolus acutifolius) major globulin|journal=Food Chemistry|volume=50|issue=3|pages=261–266|doi=10.1016/0308-8146(94)90130-9|url=https://doi.org/10.1016/0308-8146(94)90130-9|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Tepary beans contain higher levels of essential minerals than common pinto beans, with levels 10–40% higher. The exceptions are [[iron]], [[nickel]] and [[selenium]], for which the content is the same in both types of bean. There are also differences in the levels of some trace elements, with tepary beans having lower levels of [[rubidium]] but higher levels of [[bromine]] and [[strontium]] than pinto beans. <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Calloway|first1=D.H.|last2=Giauque|first2=R.D.|last3=Costa|first3=F.M.|year=1974|title=The superior mineral content of some American Indian foods in comparison to federally donated counterpart commodities|journal=Ecology of Food and Nutrition|volume=3|issue=3|pages=203–211|doi=10.1080/03670244.1974.9990382 |bibcode=1974EcoFN...3..203C }}</ref>

Tepary beans are, however, relatively low in the sulfur-containing amino acids [[cysteine]], [[methionine]], and also [[tryptophan]], likewise as the common bean and other legume crops.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Nosworthy|first=Matthew G.|year=2020|title=Enhancing Pulse Protein Quality through Processing and Genetic Tools|journal=Cereal Foods World|volume=65|issue=2|pages=54–61|doi=10.1094/CFW-65-2-0015|url=https://www.cerealsgrains.org/publications/cfw/2020/Documents/CFW-65-2-0015.pdf}}</ref> In traditional food systems where beans form a dietary staple, these shortcomings are typically balanced by complementary foods such as maize or squash.<ref>{{cite report |last=Rose|first=Victoria|title=Tepary Bean: Nutritious and Drought-Hardy Crop for Climate Adaptation in Mesoamerica|publisher=Bioversity International and Universidad del Valle|year=2019|url=https://cgspace.cgiar.org/items/290d998d-f9b3-436e-93ac-097fa6c65457|access-date=2025-11-09}}</ref>

Anti-nutritional factors in tepary beans include [[trypsin inhibitors]] and [[lectins]], which can interfere with digestion by reducing nutrient absorption in the intestine. Trypsin inhibitor activity is largely inactivated by heat treatment, and lectins in properly cooked beans do not pose nutritional concerns.<ref name="Thorn1983" />

== Usage as fodder crop ==
In addition to its use as a dry grain for human consumption, the tepary bean has also been evaluated as a short-duration forage crop suitable for [[fodder]] production under drought conditions.<ref name="Bhardwaj20132">{{cite journal |last=Bhardwaj|first=Harbans L.|year=2013|title=Preliminary Evaluation of Tepary Bean (Phaseolus acutifolius A. Gray) as a Forage Crop|journal=Journal of Agricultural Science|volume=5|issue=7|pages=160–169|doi=10.5539/jas.v5n7p160|doi-access=free}}</ref> For use as fodder crop the aboveground biomass is cut and dried in the same way as is done for the production of other types of [[hay]].

The forage quality of tepary bean was reported to be comparable to that of alfalfa hay and soybean forage, containing about 21% crude protein and roughly 41% [[neutral detergent fiber]] (NDF).<ref name="Bhardwaj20132" />

Field trials in Virginia, United States, reported dry matter yields of approximately 4.4 t/ha from a single harvest of 59-day-old plants. By comparison, typical [[alfalfa]] (''Medicago sativa'') hay yields in the same region are around 6.7 t/ha per year, though the latter are obtained from multiple harvests during the year.<ref>{{cite web |title=2024 State Agriculture Overview: Virginia|url=https://www.nass.usda.gov/Quick_Stats/Ag_Overview/stateOverview.php?state=VIRGINIA|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture – National Agricultural Statistics Service|accessdate=2025-11-08}}</ref>

== Medical uses ==
Research in the United States and Mexico suggests that [[lectin]] toxins and other compounds from tepary beans may be useful in chemotherapy for treating cancer. However, further research is needed.<ref name="AgIndia">{{cite web |url=http://www.agriculturalproductsindia.com/cereals-pulses/cereals-tepary-bean.html|title=Tepary Bean|publisher=Agro Products|website=agriculturalproductsindia.com|access-date=2012-07-08|archive-date=2012-07-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120706102537/http://www.agriculturalproductsindia.com/cereals-pulses/cereals-tepary-bean.html}}</ref>

extract: Phaseolus acutifolius, also known as the tepary bean, is a legume native to the southwestern United States and Mexico that has been grown there by the native peoples since pre-Columbian times. It is more drought-resistant than the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) and is grown in desert and semi-desert conditions from Arizona through Mexico to Costa Rica. The water requirements are low. The crop will grow in areas where annual rainfall is less than 400 mm (16 in).
